newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn parties still far apart on tax issue.
newsitem.headline: Bonn parties still far apart on tax issue.

text.p: German government and opposition politicians failed to narrow their differences on Thursday morning in a round of discussions over the tax bill for 1997, sources close to the participants said.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) are hoping to revive the wealth tax in some form, perhaps for individuals, but the coalition Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats rejected the proposal, the sources said.
Talks broke at midday for separate discussions.
The wealth tax will lapse at the end of this year as a result of a Constitutional Court decision.

About 3.0 billion marks ($2 billion) a year must be found to make up the revenues lost to state coffers, said Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber of the CSU. Most state governments are controlled by the SPD.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel has vowed to bring Germany's public sector deficit below three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for the single European currency. He has lowered the target for the federal deficit and turned up the heat on the states to keep their budgets in line as well.
Before the talks began, Hans-Peter Repnik, deputy leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary faction, declined to comment on the subject of the wealth tax except to say there was nothing to discuss.
Hamburg's SPD mayor Henning Voscherau said the lapse of the wealth tax was unacceptable, and that it should be retained for private taxpayers.
